en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Bhūtagāmavagga 19.
The Training Rule on Large Viharas.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Monastery.
Now at that time, a high official who was the attendant of the Venerable Channa was having a dwelling built for him.
Then the Venerable Channa had the dwelling roofed again and again and plastered again and again once it was finished;
the dwelling collapsed from being overburdened.
Then the Venerable Channa, while gathering grass and wood, damaged a certain brahmin’s barley field.
Thereupon, that brahmin complained, grumbled,
and became indignant, saying, “How can these venerable sirs damage our barley field?”
The monks heard that brahmin complaining, grumbling, and lamenting.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... they complained, grumbled, and lamented:
"How can the Venerable Channa have a monastery that has already been finished built over and over again, and have it plastered over and over again, until the overburdened monastery collapses?"
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked the Venerable Channa in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“… ‘Is it true, Channa, that you had a completed dwelling roofed over again and again, and plastered again and again, so that the dwelling, being overburdened, collapsed?
‘It is true, Blessed One.’”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, have a monastery roofed again and again and plastered again and again once the construction is finished? The monastery, being overburdened, collapses.
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:

“When a monk is having a large dwelling built, he should determine its extent up to the door-frames, the setting of the bolts, the preparation of the windows, and the space for two or three layers of roofing, while standing on ground that is not overgrown with grass.
Should he exceed that limit, even if it is on ground not overgrown with grass, [he commits an offense].”
"If one stands [and] makes a formal resolve, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
A "large dwelling" (mahallaka) is said to be one that has an owner.
A "vihāra" means it is either plastered on the inside, plastered on the outside, or plastered both inside and outside.
"By one who is having it built" means...
Whether doing it oneself or having it done by another.
"As far as the door-frame" means within arm’s reach all around the wooden door-panels.
"For the purpose of fixing the bolt" means for the purpose of fixing the door.
"For the preparation of the light-opening" means...
For the work of whitewashing the windows, there is the application of white color, black color, red ocher, floral designs, creeper designs, shark-tooth patterns, and the fivefold border.
Regarding the rule that one standing on non-green ground must determine the turn for two or three layers of roofing:
"green" means grain that has already ripened or grain that has not yet ripened.
If he resolves while standing on greenery, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For one covering with a path, having resolved two paths, he should depart after commanding a third path.
For one covering by turns, having resolved two turns, he should depart after commanding a third turn.
If, standing even further away than that, in a place devoid of vegetation, one should resolve [to build],
then for one covering with bricks, there is an offense of pācittiya for each brick;
for one covering with stone, there is an offense of pācittiya for each stone.
For one covering with plaster, there is an offense of expiation for every lump.
For one covering with grass, there is an offense of expiation for every blade.
For one covering with leaves, there is an offense of expiation for every leaf.
If it has been more than two or three times and he perceives it as more than that, and he makes a formal determination, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If it has been more than two or three times and he is uncertain, and he makes a formal determination, there is an offense of expiation.
If it has been more than two or three times and he perceives it as less than that, and he makes a formal determination, there is an offense of expiation.
If it is less than twenty-two recitations and he perceives it as more, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is less than twenty-two recitations and he is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is less than twenty-two recitations and he perceives it as less, there is no offense.
There is no offense:
if it is two or three times,
or less than two or three times.
In a shelter, in a cave,
or in a grass hut.
If it is for the sake of another,
with one's own wealth,
there is no offense anywhere except in the case of a dwelling house.
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The ninth training rule concerning large dwellings is finished.
